title: The Poisson distribution: counts of events at a steady rate

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A Poisson process produces events one at a time, in time or in space, under three conditions. Events happen at a constant average rate. The numbers of events in intervals that do not overlap are independent. Two events at exactly the same instant do not happen.

Let X be the number of events in a fixed interval of the process. The average number of events in that interval is written with the Greek letter lambda, λ. X then has a Poisson distribution with parameter λ. For k = 0, 1, 2 and so on, with no upper limit:

P(X = k) = e(−λ) × λk ÷ k!

E[X] = λ
Var(X) = λ
SD(X) = √λ

The Poisson distribution is the limit of the binomial distribution of section 12 when the number of trials n grows and the probability p shrinks, with np held at λ. So a binomial count with large n and small p is close to a Poisson count with λ = np.

Counts whose variance is well above their mean are called overdispersed.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
Some events turn up one at a time, at a steady average rate, each without regard to the others.

The Poisson distribution gives the chance of each count, 0, 1, 2 and so on. It needs one number, the average count, λ. Its spread is set by the same number: the variance is λ too.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Start with a remark you will hear. A cardiologist looks at one day’s admissions and says: “Nine heart attacks today. We average about four. Something is going on.”

OpenIntro Statistics (https://www.openintro.org/book/os/), §4.5, gives the numbers for a real setting. About 8 million people live in New York City. Admissions for acute myocardial infarction, a heart attack, average about 4.4 a day by historical records. Take that estimate as λ, the average count for one day. Work out the chance of each count, starting from 0.

P(X = 0) = e(−4.4) = 0.0123

Each later chance is the one before times λ ÷ k. That is the formula: going from k − 1 to k multiplies in one more λ and divides by one more k.

P(X = 1) = 0.0123 times 4.4 = 0.054
P(X = 2) = 0.054 times 4.4 divided by 2 = 0.1188

Carry on the same way, keeping full precision in the calculator.

count k P(X = k)
0    0.0123
1    0.0540
2    0.1188
3    0.1743
4    0.1917
5    0.1687
6    0.1237
7    0.0778
8    0.0428
9    0.0209
10    0.0092
11    0.0037
12    0.0013

The counts 0 to 8 add up to 0.9642. So the chance of 9 or more on a given day is 1 − 0.9642, which is 0.0358. That is rare for one day. Now count the days in a year.

1 minus 0.9642 = 0.0358
365 times 0.0358 = 13.07

A city with a perfectly steady rate of 4.4 expects about 13 days a year with nine or more heart-attack admissions. Nine on one day is not a signal on its own. Two such days in a row are rarer. A year has 364 pairs of days next to each other.

0.0358 times 0.0358 = 0.00128
364 times 0.00128 = 0.47

So expect one such pair about every two years. A run longer or more frequent than that is the thing to look into.

Check the spread against the data. OpenIntro’s year of 365 daily counts has a mean of 4.38 and a standard deviation of about 2. The Poisson standard deviation is √4.4, which is 2.10. The data spread about as much as the model says they should.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
OpenIntro says its 365 daily counts are simulated, and that in practice “we should check for an association between successive days”. The 4.4 is a real historical average for one city. Heat waves, festivals and weekends can change the rate. Then a single λ for every day is wrong, and the 13 days a year is wrong with it.

The 0.0358 is the chance for one day picked before you look. It is not the chance that “something is going on” on a day you noticed because it was high.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Where does the formula come from? Build it from the binomial of section 12. The numbers here are bare: an average of 2 events in an interval.

Cut the interval into n short slices. Make them short enough that two events in one slice never happen. Then each slice is a trial: one event, a success, or none. The average is 2 events across n slices, so each slice has p = 2 ÷ n. Independence across slices is the second condition of the process. So the count is binomial, with n trials and p = 2 ÷ n.

Start with no events at all: every slice fails.

P(X = 0) = (1 − 2 ÷ n)n

Watch it as the slices get thinner.

slices n P(X = 0)
10    0.1074
100    0.1326
1000    0.1351
10000    0.1353

The values settle at 0.1353, which is e(−2). For any average λ, (1 − λ ÷ n)n settles at e(−λ) as n grows. You can watch it happen on a calculator; the proof is beyond this book.

Now the step from one count to the next. For the binomial, divide the chance of k successes by the chance of k − 1, both from the formula of section 12. Take the two pieces in turn.

The counting pieces first. Write k! as k × (k − 1)!, and (n − k + 1)! as (n − k + 1) × (n − k)!. Then everything cancels except two factors.

(n choose k) ÷ (n choose (k − 1)) = [n! ÷ (k! (n − k)!)] × [(k − 1)! (n − k + 1)! ÷ n!] = (n − k + 1) ÷ k

The powers next. The top has one more p and one fewer (1 − p) than the bottom. So the ratio of the powers is p ÷ (1 − p). Together:

P(X = k) ÷ P(X = k − 1) = [(n − k + 1) ÷ k] × [p ÷ (1 − p)]

Put p = λ ÷ n. When n is huge, n − k + 1 is almost n, and 1 − p is almost 1. So the ratio is almost n ÷ k × λ ÷ n, which is λ ÷ k. Starting from e(−λ) and multiplying by λ ÷ 1, then λ ÷ 2, up to λ ÷ k gives the formula.

P(X = k) = e(−λ) × (λ ÷ 1) × (λ ÷ 2) × … × (λ ÷ k) = e(−λ) × λk ÷ k!

The mean and the variance come the same way. The binomial mean is np, which is λ for every n. The binomial variance is np(1 − p), which is λ × (1 − p). As p shrinks, 1 − p goes to 1, so the variance goes to λ.

How close is a real binomial? Take n = 100 and p = 0.02, so np = 2.

k binomial, n = 100 and p = 0.02 Poisson, λ = 2
0 0.1326    0.1353
1 0.2707    0.2707
2 0.2734    0.2707
3 0.1823    0.1804
4 0.0902    0.0902
5 0.0353    0.0361
6 0.0114    0.0120
7 0.0031    0.0034

No pair differs by more than 0.003. That is why a count of rare events among many people, such as new cases of a disease in a large district in a month, is usually treated as a Poisson count. Nobody needs to know n or p, only their product.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: The match needs p small. With n = 10 and p = 0.2, np is still 2, but the binomial chance of no events is 0.810, about 0.107, against the Poisson’s 0.135. And a binomial count can never exceed n; a Poisson count has no ceiling. The approximation is for rare events among many trials.

blocks.label: Illustration 3
blocks.html:
Now a count that is not Poisson. A primary health centre logs new diagnoses of diabetes each day for ten days. The counts are made up for this example.

day new diagnoses
1 0
2 0
3 1
4 0
5 9
6 0
7 0
8 8
9 1
10 1

The mean is 20 ÷ 10, which is 2 a day. Work out the sample variance as in Book 0, D5, dividing by n − 1. The squared deviations from 2 are 4, 4, 1, 4, 49, 4, 4, 36, 1 and 1.

4 plus 4 plus 1 plus 4 plus 49 plus 4 plus 4 plus 36 plus 1 plus 1 = 108
108 divided by 9 = 12

A Poisson count with mean 2 has variance 2. These counts have variance 12, six times as much. They are overdispersed.

Ask what happened on days 5 and 8. Suppose they were screening-camp days, when the centre tested many more people. Then the rate was not constant. It was low on ordinary days and high on camp days. Two Poisson counts, one for each kind of day, may each fit. One Poisson count for every day does not.

Never fit a single Poisson to these data and call the camp days “unusual”. With λ = 2, the chance of 8 or more on one day is about 0.0011. That number answers a question about a steady rate that the centre never had.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: Ten days are few. A variance of 12 against a mean of 2 is a strong hint here only because the two big days stand far apart from the rest, and a reason for them is known. With ten counts that differ less, the sample variance itself scatters widely, and a gap between it and the mean proves little. Methods that model the extra spread are taught with regression models in a later book of the course.

points.html: A steady Poisson process throws up high days by chance. Before you call a day unusual, work out how often such a day comes by chance across all the days you looked at.
Before you use a Poisson model, set the variance of the counts beside their mean. If the variance is well above the mean, the events cluster or the rate changes.

The Poisson model holds only while the rate is steady and the events are independent. When the counts spread well beyond their mean, split the intervals by what changes the rate, as with the camp days, or leave it to a model for extra spread.
λ belongs to an interval. An average of 12 an hour is λ = 2 for ten minutes and λ = 288 for a day. Rescale λ to the interval you are asking about before you use the formula.

Look at many places, or many months, and one of them will show a “cluster” by chance. If one place has chance q, the chance that at least one of k independent places shows it is 1 minus (1 − q)k, the no-success chance of section 13.
The standard deviation of a Poisson count is √λ. So a count of 4 can easily move by 2. Do not read a jump from 2 to 4 cases as “doubling” without that spread in mind.

blocks.label: Common misreading
blocks.html: “λ is 4.4, the city’s historical average.” The 4.4 is an average of past days. It estimates λ, as OpenIntro’s simulated year gives 4.38. λ itself is a parameter of a model, the steady rate the model assumes. Treat any λ you read as an estimate, and ask over how many days it was counted and whether the rate was steady across them.

blocks.prompt: From memory: what three conditions make a count of events Poisson? Write the formula for P(X = k). What are its mean and its variance? What does it mean when a set of counts has a variance well above its mean?
blocks.answer:
Events happen at a constant average rate; counts in intervals that do not overlap are independent; two events never happen at exactly the same instant.

P(X = k) = e(−λ) × λk ÷ k!, for k = 0, 1, 2 and so on. Here λ is the average count in the interval.

The mean and the variance are both λ, so the standard deviation is √λ.

A variance well above the mean is overdispersion. The events cluster, or the rate changes between intervals, so the single-rate Poisson model does not fit.

blocks.prompt: For a journalist, three minutes. A district reports four new childhood cancers in one block in a year. A block of that size averages about one a year. The numbers are made up. The reporter asks you whether this is a cluster. Say what you would want to know before answering, and give one sentence they could quote.
blocks.answer:
What to say, in plain words. Rare events at a steady rate do bunch up by chance. With an average of one a year, a block has about a 1.9 per cent chance of four or more in a given year. That sounds small. But a district has many blocks, and each one has that chance every year. Across 50 blocks you would expect about one block like this in a typical year, with no cause at all.

What I would want to know. How many blocks and years were looked at before this one was noticed? Do the four cases share anything beyond the place, such as a type of cancer or a time? Has the block’s population grown?

A sentence to quote: “Four cases where we expect one is worth checking. On its own it does not show a cause, because chance alone produces a block like this somewhere in most years.”

The working is for you, not for the reporter. At λ = 1, the chance of 0, 1, 2 or 3 cases is e(−1) × (1 + 1 + 1/2 + 1/6), which is 0.9810. So P(X ≥ 4) is about 0.019, and 50 times 0.019 is 0.95. The 50 blocks are an assumption for the example; use the district’s real number.

blocks.prompt:
X has a Poisson distribution with λ = 3.

Work out P(X = 0) and P(X = 2).
blocks.answer:
P(X = 0) = e(−3) = 0.049787
P(X = 2) = e(−3) × 32 ÷ 2!
0.049787 times 9 divided by 2 = 0.2240

P(X = 0) is about 0.0498 and P(X = 2) is about 0.2240.

blocks.prompt:
X has a Poisson distribution with λ = 3.

Work out P(X ≤ 2) and P(X ≥ 3).
blocks.answer:
Add the first three chances. P(X = 1) is e(−3) × 3.

0.049787 times 3 = 0.1494

0.0498 plus 0.1494 plus 0.2240 = 0.4232
1 minus 0.4232 = 0.5768

P(X ≤ 2) is 0.4232 and P(X ≥ 3) is 0.5768. “3 or more” has no upper end, so work it out as 1 minus the chance of 0, 1 or 2.

blocks.prompt: Events happen at an average of 12 an hour, at a steady rate. Work out λ for a 10-minute interval, and the chance of no events in 10 minutes.
blocks.answer:
12 times 10 divided by 60 = 2
e(−2) = 0.1353

λ is 2 for ten minutes, and the chance of none is 0.1353.

blocks.prompt:
For a Poisson count with λ = 2.5, work out P(X = 4) divided by P(X = 3), without working out either chance.

Then, for a different Poisson count, P(X = 0) is 0.05. Work out λ.
blocks.answer:
Each chance is the one before times λ ÷ k.

2.5 divided by 4 = 0.625

The ratio is 0.625.

For the second count, P(X = 0) = e(−λ) = 0.05. Take natural logarithms of both sides, as in Book 2, section 4: −λ = ln 0.05, so λ = ln 20.

1 divided by 0.05 = 20
ln 20 = 2.996

λ is about 3.0.

blocks.prompt: OpenIntro gives about 4.4 heart-attack admissions a day in New York City. Treat the daily count as Poisson with λ = 4.4. Work out the chance of a day with no admissions, and how many such days a year to expect.
blocks.answer:
e(−4.4) = 0.01228
365 times 0.01228 = 4.48

The chance of a day with none is about 0.0123. Expect about 4 or 5 such days in a year of 365. A day with no heart attacks in the city is as much a product of chance as a day with nine.

blocks.prompt:
OpenStax Introductory Statistics 2e, §4.6, uses a reported 1.02 per cent chance of low seismic activity in a 48-hour period, over the next 200 days. Treat the count of days with low activity as binomial with n = 200 and p = 0.0102.

Work out the Poisson λ that approximates it. Then work out the chance of no such day both ways, binomial and Poisson. OpenStax uses the 48-hour chance as each day’s chance; do the same.
blocks.answer:
200 times 0.0102 = 2.04

λ is 2.04. No days with low activity means 200 failures in the binomial.

(1 − 0.0102)200 = 0.9898200 = 0.1287
e(−2.04) = 0.1300

Binomial 0.1287, Poisson 0.1300. They differ in the third decimal place, because p is small and n is large.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke.

Leah receives about 6 calls between 8 a.m. and 10 a.m.
question: the chance of more than one call in the next 15 minutes
λ = 6
P(X > 1) = 1 − P(X = 0) − P(X = 1)
= 1 − e(−6) − 6 × e(−6) = 1 − 0.0025 − 0.0149 = 0.9826
blocks.answer:
The third line broke. λ = 6 is the average for two hours. The question is about 15 minutes, one eighth of two hours.

6 divided by 8 = 0.75
e(−0.75) = 0.4724
0.75 times 0.4724 = 0.3543
1 minus 0.4724 minus 0.3543 = 0.1733

The chance is about 0.173, as OpenStax gives it (0.1734 by calculator), not 0.983.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable: 6 is the only rate in the question, and the formula accepts any λ. Nothing in the arithmetic warns you. Only the interval does.

blocks.prompt:
Here is a worked answer. Find the step that broke. The counts are made up.

new diagnoses a day for ten days: 0, 0, 1, 0, 9, 0, 0, 8, 1, 1
mean = 2 a day, so model the daily count as Poisson with λ = 2
P(X ≥ 8) at λ = 2 is about 0.0011
so days 5 and 8 are extraordinary events that need explaining
blocks.answer:
The second line broke. It chose a Poisson model without checking the spread. The sample variance of the ten counts is 108 divided by 9, which is 12. A Poisson count with mean 2 has variance 2.

108 divided by 9 = 12
12 divided by 2 = 6

The counts spread six times as much as a Poisson count would. The rate was not steady. So the 0.0011 is a chance under a model the data reject, and it says nothing about days 5 and 8.

Why it looks reasonable: the mean is right, and the formula for P(X ≥ 8) is applied correctly. The flaw is the model, not the arithmetic. If those were camp days, they need no “explaining” beyond the camp.

blocks.prompt:
A district officer writes: “Three children were newly diagnosed with type 1 diabetes in one block last month. That block averages 0.5 a month. This is a cluster and needs a field investigation.”

The district has 30 blocks of about the same size, each averaging 0.5 a month. All the numbers are made up. Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
Compute the chance of 3 or more in one block in one month, then the chance that at least one of 30 blocks shows it.

e(−0.5) = 0.6065
0.6065 times 0.5 = 0.3033
0.3033 times 0.5 divided by 2 = 0.0758
1 minus 0.6065 minus 0.3033 minus 0.0758 = 0.0144

For one block named in advance, the chance is about 0.014. Now all 30 blocks, if they are independent.

1 minus 0.0144 = 0.9856
0.985630 = 0.6472
1 minus 0.6472 = 0.3528

About a 35 per cent chance that some block in the district shows three or more in a given month. Over a year of months it becomes very likely.

What this does not establish. It does not show the three cases are chance; it shows chance is a reasonable explanation. Whether to investigate turns on other facts: whether the children share an exposure, a type, or a week of onset. And the 0.5 a month is itself an estimate from past years, not a known λ.

blocks.prompt:
The clinic has averaged 4 new hypertension diagnoses a month over the past three years. This month there were 8. The clinic newsletter says: “New hypertension diagnoses doubled. Hypertension is rising fast in our area.” The numbers are made up.

Decide what to compute, compute it, and say what your answer does not establish.
blocks.answer:
Ask how surprising 8 would be if nothing had changed. Take the three-year average of 4 as λ.

e(−4) = 0.0183

The chances of 0 to 7 are 0.0183, 0.0733, 0.1465, 0.1954, 0.1954, 0.1563, 0.1042 and 0.0595.

0.0183 plus 0.0733 plus 0.1465 plus 0.1954 plus 0.1954 plus 0.1563 plus 0.1042 plus 0.0595 = 0.9489
1 minus 0.9489 = 0.0511

With a steady λ of 4, a month of 8 or more comes about one month in 20. With a standard deviation of √4, which is 2, a count of 8 is two standard deviations above 4.

What this does not establish. One month of 8 does not show the rate doubled. It also says nothing about the area. Diagnoses depend on how many people were screened. A camp or a new blood-pressure machine raises them with no change in anyone’s blood pressure. A “rise in hypertension” needs a prevalence, with a denominator.
